messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 41

**Case Vignette: "Matthew"**

Matthew is a 32-year-old park ranger who has been single since his early twenties. He presents as lean and physically fit, with a guarded but polite demeanor. He arrives for sessions directly from work, often still wearing his uniform shirt, and he sits with his back to the wall, his eyes scanning the room once before settling on the floor.

The trauma happened four years ago, during a solo backcountry patrol in a remote national forest. Matthew had responded to a report of illegal camping. He found three men at a site that had been used for weeks. They were hostile, and when he attempted to radio for backup, they overpowered him. For the next 18 hours, they held him in a shallow cave. They bound his hands and feet with paracord. They beat him systematically, focusing on his ribs and kidneys. They burned his forearms with the end of a hot camp stove. They forced him to drink muddy water. They told him, repeatedly, that no one would find him, that the forest would swallow him. He remembers the smell of pine duff and propane. He remembers the sound of his own teeth chattering against the cold ground.

He was found the next afternoon by a search team. He was hypothermic, dehydrated, and had three cracked ribs. The men were arrested. Matthew spent three days in a hospital. He was given a clean bill of physical health within two months. But the psychological aftermath has been relentless.

In the present, Matthew still works as a ranger, but he no longer takes solo patrols. He volunteered for a desk shift twice a week, handling permits and visitor questions. This feels like a demotion, but he cannot bring himself to go into the backcountry alone. When he drives a patrol truck through dense forest, his heart rate spikes. He checks his rearview mirror constantly. He has to pull over and breathe when the road narrows between two rock outcroppings, because the shape of the cave wall comes back to him.

He has not told his coworkers the full story. They know he was assaulted. They do not know the details. When someone at the station jokes about the "bad campers" they’ve dealt with, Matthew’s stomach turns. He excuses himself. He has started taking the long way to the bathroom to avoid walking past the evidence locker where his torn uniform was stored.

At home, in his small apartment, he keeps the lights on all night. He sleeps on the couch, facing the door. He has not had a romantic relationship since the attack. He tried dating once, six months ago. The woman touched his forearm during dinner, and he flinched so hard he knocked over his water glass. He made an excuse and left. He now avoids physical contact with anyone.

He drinks three or four beers every night to quiet the intrusive images. He has nightmares three or four times a week. In the dreams, he is always in the cave, but the men are faceless, and his radio is dead. He wakes up gasping, his hands clenched into fists. He has not been able to sit with his back to a door in a restaurant or a coffee shop since the attack.

Matthew’s score on the PCL-5 is 41, indicating a high level of PTSD symptom severity. He reported that the worst part of his day is the quiet hour before sunset, when the light in his apartment turns the color of the cave entrance. He has not told anyone this.
